# Implement block: Glass Marbles Tray (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Glass Marbles Tray" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

Thirteen glass marbles rest in the carved cups of a walnut tray on a dark table: twelve cat's-eyes in cobalt, amber, emerald, oxblood, milk, violet, aqua, smoke, honey, rose, lime and indigo, and one larger shooter striped red and yellow. Each marble is clear at its centre and thick with colour at its rim, its swirl of leaf-shaped vanes sits inside the glass, light gathers on its far side and a sharp highlight and a small window reflection catch the light; its shadow falls to the lower right, tinted by its glass, with a bright coloured caustic inside it. The tray has a mitred frame with bevelled edges and brass pins and a pale oak floor with a honeycomb of shallow cups. Small capitals read "Parlour games · No. 4" at the top left beside a live tilt readout ("10.8°"); "Glass Marbles" sits in a serif at the bottom over a line of copy and the hint "Drag to tilt · Shake to scatter · Tap a marble". Everything is drawn: no photos.

**Motion.** One clock drives everything: ticks of 1/60 s, at most three a frame, each split into two collision substeps. Dragging presses the tray down where the finger goes: it tilts in perspective (eye 900 pt above it) towards that side, up to 0.24 rad along a tanh of the drag (three quarters of the way at 150 pt), and slides with the finger by 7% up to 16 pt; the tilt follows on a spring (150/s², 17/s) and the slide on a stiffer one (260/s², 24/s), and on release both spring back carrying their speed. The marbles roll downhill under 4300 pt/s² times the floor's slope, feel the tray's acceleration as it slides, keep 70% of their speed per second plus a 16 pt/s² rolling friction, and settle in the cups, which pull them to their centres like 1.4 pt deep bowls with extra damping (2.4/s), so a tilt past about 9° rolls them out. They collide as circles with mass by volume and restitution 0.82, bounce off the wooden walls and rounded corners at 0.45, and every click faster than 170 pt/s flashes a small four-pointed glint for 0.22 s and, while the user plays, a selection haptic (rigid above 420 pt/s, at most one each 90 ms). Each marble carries a 3D orientation that turns about the axis across its path by distance over radius, so its swirl visibly rolls. A finger that reverses twice within 0.5 s faster than 1000 pt/s is a shake: every marble is knocked 220 to 480 pt/s in a seeded random direction and hops up to 340 pt/s, lifting off the floor with its shadow spreading and landing under 5200 pt/s² gravity, with a medium haptic. Tapping a marble flicks it away from the finger at 620 pt/s with a small hop and a light haptic. The light moves with the tilt, so shadows and caustics slide across the floor. The self-playing demo loops every 12 s: level at first, the tilt traces one and a quarter circles from 1 to 7 s rising and falling to 0.2 rad, the tray jolts sideways five times a second for 0.7 s at 7.5 s while the marbles scatter, then from 8.7 s each marble is led back to its own cup (a spring of 16/s² and 5/s, at full strength by 10.4 s) and the last 1.1 s ease them onto the exact resting state. A touch stops it for 3.5 s. Under reduced motion the demo does not play, the tilt reaches 45% as far without sliding, a shake knocks at 35% and a flick at half speed.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [GlassMarblesTrayDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Playground/GlassMarblesTray/GlassMarblesTrayDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [GlassMarblesTray.metal](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Playground/GlassMarblesTray/GlassMarblesTray.metal)
- [GlassMarblesTray.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Playground/GlassMarblesTray/GlassMarblesTray.swift)
- [GlassMarblesTrayEngine.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Playground/GlassMarblesTray/GlassMarblesTrayEngine.swift)
- [GlassMarblesTrayPainter.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Playground/GlassMarblesTray/GlassMarblesTrayPainter.swift)
- [GlassMarblesTraySim.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Playground/GlassMarblesTray/GlassMarblesTraySim.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
